artifacts.summary: Re-derived, verified inventory of every file needing a change to remove the per-dispatch worktree isolation layer: corrects the dispatch's named footprint (10 false-positive files, 4 missing test files carrying ~118 references), flags a dual-purpose function that must be renamed not deleted, two correctness fixes the removal enables, a repo-root .gitignore edit outside the source store, and honest pre-removal byte-budget baselines for the SKILL.md ceiling and eager-load gates.

memory_candidates.content: When a dispatch's description names a mechanically-counted reference inventory (e.g. 'N references across M files' from a grep) as the removal footprint, re-derive it before trusting it. In one case, 10 of ~18 named files were false positives (generic git-worktree or unrelated-parameter prose matching the same grep terms) and 4 files carrying ~118 real references were missing entirely because the original count only grepped a narrower term set. Re-grep with the exact literal dependency string (e.g. the script's filename) separately from the broad conceptual term to separate hard dependencies from incidental prose hits.

Before deleting a function slated for removal as part of a feature teardown, enumerate ALL of its call sites, not just the ones belonging to the feature being removed. A function can be dual-purpose: here, task_selected_for_worktree_isolation() was built for worktree-isolation selection but was later reused, unchanged, as the sole array-membership reader for an unrelated co-scheduling admission rule. Deleting the function wholesale would have silently broken the surviving feature. The fix is rename-and-narrow (keep the function, drop only the call sites belonging to the removed feature) rather than delete-and-recreate.

A byte-budget gate (SKILL.md ceiling, eager-context-load baseline) should not be assumed to gain headroom from a removal just because the removal deletes a lot of text somewhere in the repo -- check whether the specific edited files are actually part of that gate's measured set. In one case, an eager-context-load gate was assumed to improve from a large documentation/code removal, but none of the removed/edited files were in the eager-loaded set (CLAUDE.md merge sources, eagerly-loaded rules) at all, so that gate's number was provably unaffected while a separate ceiling gate (a specific skill file) was genuinely affected. Verify gate membership before claiming a gate will improve.
